newsitem.title: USA: Newspaper says Soviet nuclear warheads broke open.
newsitem.headline: Newspaper says Soviet nuclear warheads broke open.

text.p: Nuclear warheads on a Soviet submarine that sank in 1986 broke open, spilling unknown amounts of radioactive plutonium into the Atlantic Ocean, the San Francisco Examiner reported on Sunday.
The Examiner said the spillage of the super-deadly element was one of the Cold War's darkest secrets, only now revealed.

Despite Soviet and U.S. assurances at the time that there was no radioactive contamination, the Examiner said it had learned this was the first case in which weapons-grade plutonium leaked from a submarine into the ocean.

"We are aware of the fact that the warheads are destroyed, but how far the plutonium has gone, it's not known," the newspaper quoted Stanislav Vesnovskii, a top scientist at Arzamas-16, one of Russia's two main nuclear weapons laboratories, as saying.
It quoted Vesnovskii as saying that one warhead was destroyed by an explosion on the sub and others were destroyed by high pressure as the sub sank into deep water.
The Soviet submarine, called K-219, sank in the Atlantic Ocean 600 miles (960 kms) east of Bermuda in October 1986, dragging down four crew members and 32 nuclear warheads.

As the sub sank, the nuclear warheads, which contained an estimated 200 pounds (90 kg) of radioactive plutonium-239, broke open, spilling unknown amounts of the element into the sea, the Examiner said in the copyright story. The report did not say how many of the warheads broke open.
It said a secret team of Russian investigators later discovered traces of plutonium on floating submarine debris.

Top Russian and U.S. scientists do not know how far, if at all, the plutonium has travelled from the wrecked submarine, which settled 18,000 feet (5,500 metres) beneath the surface, the Examiner reported. The site is one of the deepest parts of the North Atlantic, where plutonium might tend to stay put because of slow water circulation and sticky seafloor mud, it said.

But some plutonium might also have been absorbed into the food chain in the ocean's upper layers as the sub sank, it said. If so, then particles of plutonium -- a super heavy element that causes cancer if inhaled and remains dangerously radioactive for tens of thousands of years -- may still be coursing through the bodies of fish, it said.

The report said Vesnovskii, his Russian colleagues and American scientists hope to launch a U.S.-Russian project to send an oceanographic ship to survey the sunken sub with deep- sea cameras and to gather seafloor samples. They could also assess whether the spill should be cleaned up, it said.

The main U.S. collaborators on the proposed project are Charles Hollister and Hugh Livingston, scientists at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in Massachusetts, the report said, adding that the Russians had privately asked researchers at America's Lawrence Livermore and Los Alamos nuclear weapons laboratories to join the team.
Hollister's team sent a proposal to the U.S. Navy for research funds for the project but the Navy has ignored the request, the report said.
